new.title: See how doctors learned their trade at the Alte Anatomie
new.desc: Ingolstadt was home to Bavaria's first university, and its baroque anatomy building from the 1720s now houses the Deutsches Medizinhistorisches Museum. Inside you find surgical instruments, anatomical preparations and teaching models spanning medicine from antiquity to today.
new.tip: Leave time for the medicinal herb garden behind the building, laid out like an old university physic garden. Fans of Frankenstein will enjoy knowing Mary Shelley sent her hero to study in Ingolstadt.

new.title: Look up at the giant ceiling fresco in Maria de Victoria
new.desc: This former Marian congregation hall was finished in the 1730s and blessed in 1736. Cosmas Damian Asam covered its ceiling with a 490 square metre painting, often called the largest flat ceiling fresco in the world, with the four known continents in the corners.
new.tip: Walk slowly across the room while watching the fresco, as the painted architecture shifts with your viewpoint. Ask to see the Lepanto monstrance in the sacristy, an 18 kg silver piece from 1708 showing the famous sea battle.
new.q: St. Maria de Victoria, Neubaustraße 3, Ingolstadt

new.title: Walk through the Kreuztor, Ingolstadt's landmark gate
new.desc: Built in 1385, the Kreuztor is the city's emblem: a red brick gate with slim corner turrets and a steep spire. Its name comes from a leper house of the Holy Cross that stood west of the town until it was destroyed in 1546.
new.tip: Walk round to the outside of the gate for the best photo, then follow the remains of the old fortifications along the green belt.

new.title: Meet Franz Marc's animals above the Kochelsee
new.desc: The Franz Marc Museum in Kochel am See shows the Blue Rider painter's horses, deer and foxes alongside works by his contemporaries and later artists. Marc lived and painted in this valley, and the museum's modern wing sits on a hillside with big windows over the lake and mountains.
new.tip: Pair it with a stroll in the sculpture park around the museum, and check the website for the current special exhibition before you go.
new.q: Franz Marc Museum, Franz Marc Park 8-10, Kochel am See

new.title: Watch six giant pipes drop down at the Walchenseekraftwerk
new.desc: Since 1924 this power station has used the 201 metre drop between the Walchensee and the Kochelsee to make electricity. Six pressure pipes, each 430 metres long, run straight down the mountainside to the turbine hall, a project masterminded by Oskar von Miller.
new.tip: The visitor centre next to the turbine hall explains the whole system and is a good stop on the drive up the Kesselberg road to the Walchensee.

new.title: Step into the abbey church of Benediktbeuern
new.desc: Benediktbeuern was founded as a Benedictine abbey in the 8th century and is now run by the Salesians of Don Bosco. The baroque basilica of St. Benedikt anchors a vast cloister complex at the foot of the mountains, close to the Kochelsee.
new.tip: The famous Carmina Burana manuscript was discovered in this monastery's library in 1803. Walk out into the Loisach moorland behind the abbey for wide views of the Benediktenwand.

new.title: Learn how a violin is made in Mittenwald
new.desc: Violin making has shaped Mittenwald since Matthias Klotz brought the craft home in the late 17th century. The Geigenbaumuseum, in one of the oldest houses in town, shows baroque Mittenwald instruments, a historic workshop and listening and smelling stations for woods and varnishes.
new.tip: Afterwards look for the Klotz statue in front of the parish church, and keep an eye out for working violin makers' workshops in the side streets.

new.title: Find the cross in the lake where Ludwig II died
new.desc: King Ludwig II was found dead in the shallows of Lake Starnberg near Berg on the evening of 13 June 1886. A wooden cross now stands in the water at the spot, and on the slope above it a neo-Romanesque memorial chapel was built between 1896 and 1900.
new.tip: Walk there through the lakeside park from Berg or from Leoni. Every year around 13 June a memorial service is held here, and royalists in traditional dress turn up.

new.title: Explore the treasure house of the Freising Diözesanmuseum
new.desc: On the cathedral hill in Freising, the archdiocese of Munich and Freising shows one of the largest church art collections anywhere, with works from late antiquity to contemporary art. Highlights include Byzantine pieces, late Gothic carvings and a huge collection of nativity scenes.
new.tip: Combine it with the cathedral next door, and step onto the terrace of the hill for the view over the Isar plain toward Munich.

new.title: Wander among old planes at the Flugwerft Schleißheim
new.desc: The Deutsches Museum's aviation branch sits on one of Germany's oldest airfields, where the Royal Bavarian flying corps built its hangar and command post between 1912 and 1918. The halls hold a 1918 Fokker D.VII, a Starfighter, a MiG-21, a Eurofighter prototype and an Ariane 5 booster.
new.tip: Look into the glass restoration workshop from the gallery to watch aircraft being rebuilt. Bring a picnic: the airfield is still active, so you may see gliders take off.

new.title: Find out what makes beer bitter at the Hopfenmuseum
new.desc: Wolnzach lies in the heart of the Hallertau, the largest continuous hop growing area in the world. The Deutsches Hopfenmuseum, opened in 2002, tells the story of hop farming from the 16th century to today with pictures, documents and old tools.
new.tip: Come in late August or early September when the hop gardens are being harvested and the tall green bines are cut down around the village.

new.title: Go backstage at the Passion Play theatre in Oberammergau
new.desc: In 1633 the villagers of Oberammergau vowed to perform the suffering and death of Christ if they were spared the plague, and they have kept their promise roughly every ten years since 1634. The play runs for hours on the open air stage of the Passionstheater, with hundreds of locals in the cast.
new.tip: Between Passion years the theatre hosts other plays and concerts and offers guided tours of the stage, costume rooms and workshops. Book a tour on the theatre's website.

new.title: Stand under the Olympic ski jump in Partenkirchen
new.desc: The 1936 Winter Olympic ski jump was held on the Gudiberg, and since 1922 Partenkirchen has hosted a New Year's ski jump, now part of the Four Hills Tournament. The current jump, opened in 2007, is a sleek concrete and steel ramp with a hill size of 142 metres.
new.tip: Walk into the old Olympic stadium below the jump at any time of year. On 1 January the place fills with tens of thousands of fans, so book early if you want to watch.

new.title: Meet the royal boat Delphin at the Museum Starnberger See
new.desc: This lakeside museum tells the story of court boating and life around Lake Starnberg. Its star exhibit is the Delphin, the last surviving boat of the Bavarian royal pleasure fleet, and you can also walk through the Lochmann-Haus, an old farmhouse built into the museum.
new.tip: It opens in the afternoons midweek and from late morning at weekends. Afterwards walk down to the Seepromenade for the boat landing and a view of the Alps across the water.
new.q: Museum Starnberger See, Possenhofener Straße 5, Starnberg

new.title: Climb the Kalvarienberg above Bad Tölz
new.desc: Above the old town of Bad Tölz stands a baroque ensemble of the Holy Cross double church, the little Leonhardikapelle and stations of the cross leading up a former gallows hill. From the top you look across the Isar valley and the roofs of the Marktstraße to the mountains.
new.tip: On 6 November the famous Leonhardifahrt procession of decorated horse wagons climbs up here for the blessing of the horses, one of the most spectacular customs in Bavaria. Arrive early to find a spot on the slope.

new.title: Pass under the Schöner Turm in Erding
new.desc: The Schöne Turm, also called the Landshuter Tor, is the last surviving gate tower of Erding's town walls. It was built in 1408 in the late Gothic style of the Landshut school and got its onion dome in the 1660s after a fire in the Thirty Years' War.
new.tip: Use it as the start of a walk along the Landshuter Straße and around the old town squares, a calm contrast to the crowds at the nearby Therme.

new.title: Watch the Schuhplattler at Gasthof Fraundorfer
new.desc: This family run inn on Partenkirchen's painted Ludwigstraße has been serving Bavarian food for generations. On most evenings live music and Schuhplattler dancers in lederhosen slap their shoes and thighs between the tables, and admission is free.
new.tip: The restaurant opens in the evening only and is closed on Tuesdays and Wednesdays. Reserve a table, as the dance evenings are popular.

new.title: Have lunch at the Klosterbräustüberl Schäftlarn
new.desc: Kloster Schäftlarn, a Benedictine abbey founded in 762, sits in the Isar valley south of Munich. Its Klosterbräustüberl is a country inn with a beer garden that serves Angus beef from the landlords' own herd, fish from the nearby Aumühle and game.
new.tip: Closed on Wednesdays. Look into the rococo abbey church next door, and arrive by bike along the Isar cycle path from Munich.

new.title: Drink cloister beer with an Alpine view at Reutberg
new.desc: Franciscan nuns still live at Kloster Reutberg, on a hill above the Kirchsee near Sachsenkam. Its brewery has been making beer since 1677 and is run as a cooperative, and the Klosterbräustüberl beer garden is known for its panorama of the Alps.
new.tip: Walk the path around the Kirchsee below first, a small moor lake that is lovely for a summer swim, then climb up for a beer and a Brotzeit.

new.title: Taste beer brewed in Oberammergau at the Maxbräu
new.desc: The Ammergauer Maxbräu is a small brewery restaurant inside the Hotel Maximilian, where the beer is brewed on site. The copper kettles share the room with the tables, and the menu sticks to Bavarian dishes that go with the house beers.
new.tip: Come after a walk through the painted village or a tour of the Passionstheater, both a short stroll away. In summer there is a beer garden.

new.title: Eat under the maples at Weissbräu Huber in Freising
new.desc: Weissbräu Huber has welcomed guests in Freising since 1860, at the eastern end of the pedestrian zone. The kitchen serves Bavarian and Austrian classics with beer from the Hofbrauhaus Freising, and the garden is shaded by maple trees.
new.tip: It is open every day and the weekday lunch specials are good value. Walk up to the cathedral hill afterwards to work off the Schweinsbraten.

new.title: Try a Tölzer Prügel at Café Schuler
new.desc: Konditorei Café Schuler on Bad Tölz's sloping Marktstraße is the town's classic pastry shop, with handmade chocolates, Bienenstich and fruit tarts. Its signature is the Tölzer Prügel, a local speciality named after the town.
new.tip: Closed on Mondays. Breakfast is served until noon, and the chocolates make a good gift to take home.
new.q: Konditorei Café Schuler, Marktstraße 9, Bad Tölz

new.title: Order trout by the Isar at the Forellenhof Walgerfranz
new.desc: Just outside Bad Tölz near the Isar, the Forellenhof Walgerfranz is a country inn with its own ponds and animals. Trout is the obvious order, and in summer you eat it in the beer garden.
new.tip: Closed on Wednesdays unless it is a public holiday. It makes a good stop on a bike ride along the Isar.
new.q: Forellenhof Walgerfranz, Bairawieser Straße 43, Bad Tölz

new.title: Sit under the old trees at the Antonius-Schwaige
new.desc: The Antonius-Schwaige on the western edge of Ingolstadt is one of the oldest beer gardens in the region. Old trees shade the courtyard, and the kitchen serves Bavarian dishes and Brotzeit plates all day.
new.tip: Closed on Tuesdays, and on weekdays it opens only in the late afternoon. Reservations are by phone only.

new.title: Share a table with locals at the Kastaniengarten
new.desc: In the village of Oberhaunstadt on Ingolstadt's northern edge, the Kastaniengarten is a traditional beer garden under chestnut trees that is popular with locals. When the beer garden season ends, the restaurant inside keeps going.
new.tip: Open Wednesday to Sunday only, and on Sundays just for lunch. Book ahead for a table under the chestnuts on summer weekends.

new.title: Shop the farmers' market on Ingolstadt's Theaterplatz
new.desc: On Wednesday and Saturday mornings farmers and traders set up on the Theaterplatz in front of the brutalist city theatre. A few steps away the small daily Viktualienmarkt has stalls for Bavarian snacks and international food.
new.tip: Go before 10 on a Saturday when the stalls are full and locals do their weekly shop, then grab a Leberkässemmel at the Viktualienmarkt.

new.title: Eat in Germany and sit in Austria at the Ederkanzel
new.desc: The Berggasthaus Ederkanzel sits at 1,208 metres above Mittenwald, right on the border: the house stands in Bavaria while its terrace is on Tyrolean ground. From there you look over three valleys to the Wetterstein and Karwendel ranges.
new.tip: The paths up are easy enough for families. Order the huge pancake the house is known for, and combine the walk with the Leutaschklamm below.

new.title: Buy smoked fish from a Lake Starnberg fishing family
new.desc: The Dechant family has fished Lake Starnberg since the 15th century, and their shop on Starnberg's main street sells the catch. Fish are smoked over beech and alder wood in a traditional Altona kiln.
new.tip: Open Tuesday to Saturday. Take a smoked fish and a roll down to the lake promenade, a few minutes' walk away, for a picnic.

new.title: Float down the Isar on a timber raft
new.desc: Raftsmen once carried timber and goods down the Isar to Munich, and today big log rafts still drift the roughly 24 km from Wolfratshausen to Munich with music and a barrel of beer on board. The highlight is the Mühltal raft slide, a 345 metre chute with a 17 metre drop.
new.tip: The season runs from early May to mid September and rafts are usually booked by groups, so join a company outing or ask the operators about single seats well in advance.

new.title: Take the little ferry to the Roseninsel
new.desc: The only island in Lake Starnberg was Ludwig II's private retreat, where he received Richard Wagner and Empress Elisabeth in his small villa, the Casino. Today the villa is a museum, the rose garden blooms in summer, and the island is part of the UNESCO listed prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps.
new.tip: A small boat crosses from the Glockensteg in Feldafing in the warmer months. Walk there through the landscaped park around the Feldafing golf course.

new.title: Walk all the way round the Eibsee
new.desc: Below the north face of the Zugspitze lies the Eibsee, a clear green lake dotted with small islands. It was formed by a huge rockfall from the Zugspitze in the Bronze Age, and the boulders of that landslide are still scattered in the forest around it.
new.tip: The loop is an easy walk of around two hours. Start early in the day, as the car park fills fast in summer, or come by the Zugspitzbahn train.

new.title: Walk through the tunnels of the Höllentalklamm
new.desc: The Hammersbach has cut a narrow gorge into the Zugspitze massif, and since 1905 a path has led through it on ledges, bridges and rock tunnels. Waterfalls thunder past just a few metres away, and the route continues up toward the Höllentalangerhütte.
new.tip: It is about an hour's walk from Hammersbach to the gorge entrance, where a small fee is charged. Bring a rain jacket as the tunnels drip, and check that the gorge is open, as it closes in winter and after storms.

new.title: Cross the border through the Leutaschklamm
new.desc: The Leutascher Ache squeezes through a gorge on the Bavarian Tyrolean border just outside Mittenwald. Steel walkways added in 2006 make it the longest accessible gorge in the eastern limestone Alps, and from the Mittenwald end a plank path leads to a 23 metre waterfall.
new.tip: Walking the gorge itself is free; only the short waterfall trail charges a fee. Families will like the goblin themed loop with stations on local legends.

new.title: Look into the giant telescope on the Karwendel
new.desc: Since 1967 the Karwendelbahn has lifted visitors from Mittenwald to 2,244 metres, just below the Westliche Karwendelspitze. At the top a nature centre shaped like an enormous telescope juts out over the cliff and frames the view down onto Mittenwald.
new.tip: Go on a clear morning before the clouds build up. Sure footed hikers can follow the panorama paths around the top station, but leave the high routes to experienced mountaineers.

new.title: Hike to the Lautersee and swim in the Ferchensee
new.desc: West of Mittenwald a path climbs through the Laintal past waterfalls to the Lautersee and on to the Ferchensee, two small mountain lakes below the Wetterstein. The Ferchensee warms to over 20 degrees in summer and has very clean water, with an inn on the shore and a kiosk that rents boats.
new.tip: Make it a loop: up through the Laintal, swim, then back via the Ferchenseehöhe. On a summer weekend go early, as the lakes are a local favourite.

new.title: Spend a summer day at the Feringasee
new.desc: The Feringasee in Unterföhring is a 32 hectare lake with sandy and grassy shores, the largest bathing lake right on Munich's doorstep. Around it lie 21 hectares of lawns, and the name recalls the first record of Föhring in a document of Duke Tassilo III.
new.tip: Take the S-Bahn to Unterföhring and walk or cycle the last stretch. Weekday evenings after work are the most relaxed time to swim.

new.title: Tour the world's biggest wheat beer brewery in Erding
new.desc: Erdinger Weißbräu says it is the largest wheat beer brewery in the world, brewing all its beer in Erding and exporting it to more than 100 countries. Guided tours in German and English take you through the brewhouse and bottling halls and end with a Bavarian Brotzeit and a tasting.
new.tip: Book online in advance and allow up to three hours. The route has about 260 steps, and the bottling lines are still on Friday afternoons and Saturdays.

new.title: Hike the Maisinger Schlucht to the Maisinger See
new.desc: From the edge of Starnberg a path follows the Maisinger Bach up a wooded ravine to the Maisinger See near Pöcking. The small lake was formed by the Isar Loisach glacier at the end of the last Ice Age and is slowly silting up, which makes it a haven for birds.
new.tip: Allow about an hour each way from Starnberg station, and wear sturdy shoes as the path by the stream can be muddy.

new.title: Walk up to the Ilkahöhe above Tutzing
new.desc: The Ilkahöhe is a 726 metre moraine hill above Tutzing on the west shore of Lake Starnberg. On clear days the panorama runs from the Zugspitze to the Chiemgau Alps, with the whole lake at your feet. It is named after Princess Ilka von Wrede, honoured for nursing the wounded in the war of 1870 and 1871.
new.tip: Walk up from Tutzing station in about an hour. Come in autumn on a Föhn day, when the mountains look close enough to touch.
